name: Facial width-to-height ratio (FWHR)

card.summary: Cheekbone width divided by upper-face height; real research links it weakly to perceived dominance and aggression, and forums treat it as a masculinity and attractiveness score.
card.note: Studies of what it predicts are mixed and effect sizes are small; measurement is sensitive to camera distance and landmark choice.

quick.overview:
FWHR is the width of the face across the cheekbones divided by the height from the upper lip to the brow. Researchers have studied it since the late 2000s as a possible cue of aggression, dominance and trustworthiness, mostly in men.

Looksmaxxing communities turned it into a numeric score, with wider values often described as more masculine, and some users measure their own face from photos. Published meta-analyses report a very small sex difference and a small link with aggression, and later studies have questioned several of the findings.
quick.mechanism: The ratio is thought by some researchers to be shaped by puberty hormones and facial growth, though a study of adolescents found no association with testosterone levels. Another line of research proposes that observers over-attribute aggression to wide faces. Forum users discuss it as a fixed bony trait and ask whether anything can change it.
quick.risks: Measuring FWHR itself is harmless. Camera distance and lens changes the measured value, which users have noted. Discussion of cosmetic or hormonal ways to widen the face, including among minors, involves medical interventions whose evidence is limited; no study shows that treatments change FWHR.

lead: Facial width-to-height ratio (FWHR or fWHR) is the distance between the cheekbones (bizygomatic width) divided by the height of the upper face, typically measured between the upper lip and the brow.[1][2] It is a size-independent measure and has been studied as a possible sexually dimorphic cue linked to dominance, threat and aggression.[1][2]

A 2015 meta-analysis found the ratio was larger in men than in women, with a small effect size (d = 0.11).[1] A separate 2015 meta-analysis reported a small but significant positive relationship between men's FWHR and aggression.[2] Other work has found the link depends on factors such as income, and some studies have not replicated it.[4]

In looksmaxxing, FWHR became a standard metric. Grokipedia says community sources treat values around 1.8 or above as ideal for masculinity, while noting these are informal standards, and that scientific studies connect higher FWHR with perceived dominance and threat and often lower attractiveness ratings.[10]

paras: A 2008 study of hockey players and laboratory tasks reported that FWHR was associated with aggressive behavior.[7] A 2009 paper found observers could estimate aggression from neutral faces and that the estimates tracked FWHR.[8] A neuroimaging study reported amygdala reactivity to angry faces related to aggression only among men with larger FWHR.[3] A 2012 paper linked facial structure with unethical behavior.[9]

Later work questioned these findings. A 2018 study found FWHR was linked to dominance depending on income and testosterone and noted failures to replicate the aggression link.[4] A 2016 study found FWHR was not associated with adolescent testosterone levels, prompting commentaries and a response.[5][11] A 2023 study suggested observer bias plays a role: participants asked to draw or edit aggressive-dominant fictitious males produced faces with wider proportions.[6]

No studies found of FWHR in a clinical treatment setting, such as a trial testing an intervention that changes it. The research above is observational and experimental psychology: meta-analyses report a small sex difference and a small association with aggression in men, with mixed replication.[1][2][4]

Researchers have shown that photograph focal length changes depicted facial shape and perception.[12] A looksmax.org user reported that his FWHR measured about 1.75 to 1.8 from close range but about 2.0 from a long distance, and another replied that the measure is only useful at extremes.[13]

Users post photos for FWHR calculation, debate what counts as high or low and discuss whether bone width can change in puberty.[13] Grokipedia describes the numeric targets as informal community standards rather than validated criteria.[10]

lore.intro: FWHR is a popular scoring metric on looksmax.org, discussed alongside bone structure and measurement technique.[13]

claims.claim: A high FWHR signals masculinity and dominance.
claims.believers: Users describe wide faces as more masculine and dominant.[13][10]
claims.experts: Meta-analyses report a small sex difference and a small association with aggression, with mixed replication.[1][2][4]

claims.claim: FWHR is a precise number that can be measured from any photo.
claims.believers: Users post computed values such as 1.8.[13]
claims.experts: Research shows focal length alters depicted face shape, and a forum user reported values changing with camera distance.[12][13]

claims.claim: FWHR is set by prenatal or pubertal testosterone.
claims.believers: Community discussion often frames wide faces as an outcome of prenatal or pubertal hormones.
claims.experts: A 2016 study found no association between FWHR and adolescent testosterone levels.[5]
